stem: In physical accessibility standards, why are wheelchair ramps required to have gentle slopes (such as a maximum 1:12 ratio) and level intermediate landings?

options.text: To give people using wheelchairs room to pass someone coming the other way.
options.rationale: Passing room is set by clear-width requirements, not by slope limits or landings.

options.text: To keep the ramp within the total length allowed by building codes.
options.shortLabel: Fits within a code length limit
options.rationale: The standards limit the rise of each run, not the total length; gentle slopes make a ramp longer.

options.text: To keep the effort manageable and give users level places to rest.
options.shortLabel: Keeps climbs manageable with rest stops
options.rationale: Steep ramps are strenuous for manual wheelchair users, and intermediate landings give them level places to stop and rest.

options.text: To slow users down before they reach a busy doorway.
options.rationale: Ramp design aims to keep travel safe and manageable, not to slow people deliberately; a landing gives room to stop and manoeuvre.

explanation: Long ramps with many runs are strenuous for people using manual wheelchairs. A 1:12 maximum slope, with level landings at the top and bottom of each run, keeps the effort within range for many users and gives them places to rest; the Access Board recommends gentler slopes where space allows.

references.title: U.S. Access board: Guide to the ADA Accessibility Standards
